data.title: Finland Consumer Confidence Hits 7-month Low; Business Morale Falls Further
data.description:
HELSINKI (dpa-AFX) - Consumers in Finland remained more pessimistic in November, survey figures from Statistics Finland showed on Friday.

Separate data from the Confederation of Finnish Industries revealed that industrial sentiment declined further to the lowest level in eight months.

The consumer confidence index stood at -11.2 in November, down from -9.7 in the previous month. This was the lowest reading since April.

The survey was conducted among 1,148 persons between October 1 and 18.

Consumers' expectations regarding their own economy over the next twelve months were nearly unchanged in November, while the opinion about outlook of the general economy remained subdued.

Households viewed the current time as very unfavorable for purchasing durable goods, and spending intentions showed a clear decline. The survey indicated that households' concerns about unemployment grew slightly gloomier again in November.

The business confidence index in the manufacturing sector dropped to an 8-month low of 0 in November from 2.0 in October. Moreover, confidence is currently at its long-term average.

Production expectations for the coming months remain positive, with output volumes forecast to expand further.

Confidence in the construction sector worsened in November, while the positive sentiment of the retail sector stayed unchanged and the services sector eased compared to the prior month.

data.title: Spain's Sanchez insists he will defy polls as election campaign wraps up
data.description:
Key points:
  • Sanchez cites internal data showing Socialists leading
  • Last available polls suggest right-wing advantage
  • Combative four-way debate marked by sexism accusations
  • Parties hold closing rallies before 'reflection day'

By David Latona

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Friday he was convinced he would secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election despite adverse public polling, as the political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning ahead of Sunday's vote.

Amid a legal ban on publishing opinion surveys, the Socialist leader insisted that internal data suggested his party would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.

"I can't conceive of us losing," Sanchez told radio station SER, adding that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country's deep housing crisis.

However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People's Party and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.

TENSE DEBATE

During a four-way debate against both opposition leaders and the candidate for the hard-left Broad Front on Thursday night, Sanchez struck a more combative tone than in last week's face-off with PP chief Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who was at the time perceived as the winner.

Sanchez teamed up with his expected junior coalition partner, Broad Front's Ada Colau, to lambast Feijoo and Vox's Santiago Abascal over proposals Sanchez said represented "a return to the past".

Both Sanchez and Colau harshly criticised Abascal for refusing during the debate to condemn gender-based violence, and accused Feijoo of making a sexist remark when he referred to Colau as "the little silent one" over what he painted as her lack of criticism of the government's handling of deadly floods in 2024.

"If I have bothered anyone, I withdraw (the remark), of course," Feijoo later said, while criticising what he called the "theatrics" of his rivals.

The parties were set to hold their closing rallies on Friday evening, with the Socialists and the Broad Front choosing Madrid for their events while the PP and Vox opted for Seville and Valencia, respectively.

Spaniards observe a "day of reflection" on the eve of the vote. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

data.title: Bitcoin supply profit/loss ratio hits 11-year low as capitulation signals emerge
data.description:
Bitcoin holders are having a rough month. The seven-day moving average of Bitcoin's supply profit/loss ratio has dropped to its lowest level in 11 years, according to analysis from onchain data firm CryptoQuant.

The drop tracks the price. Bitcoin is down close to 20% month-to-date, and the onchain data shows holders absorbing that decline.

CryptoQuant described the market as being in a "meaningful stress phase" and pointed to growing evidence of seller exhaustion. That is a different diagnosis from a routine pullback, and the difference matters.

Start with the core metric. The supply profit/loss ratio compares the amount of Bitcoin currently held at a profit against the amount held at a loss.

As of late November, CryptoQuant data showed the ratio had fallen to approximately 0.8. That is clearly below the 1.0 line, so coins held at a loss now outweigh coins held at a gain.

A related figure shows the same thing. Around November 25, the share of Bitcoin supply in profit slid to 44.42%, leaving 55.58% of supply in loss.

The price explains why. Bitcoin traded in a range of roughly $58,000 to $61,000 in late November, after falling nearly 20% from its October highs.

CryptoQuant's case for seller exhaustion rests on more than one indicator. Its Sell Side Risk Ratio reached a four-year percentile near 10.1, a reading the firm associates with fading selling pressure.

The data also shows elevated realized losses and a notable drop in ETF flows. Realized losses track coins that actually changed hands below their purchase price, so rising numbers mean holders are locking in losses rather than waiting it out.

This is not the first time more than half of Bitcoin's supply has slipped into the red. Similar drops below the 50% profit threshold occurred during the 2022 bear market.

That episode lasted roughly four months before conditions recovered.

The 11-year low on the seven-day moving average gives the current reading more weight. A smoothed metric hitting its weakest level in more than a decade suggests this is not a one-day blip caused by a single sharp candle.

The confirmation signal is fairly clear. A reversal would need the profit/loss ratio and its moving averages to climb back above 1.0, along with a restored overall price structure.

When more than half of holders are sitting on unrealized losses, every rally toward their purchase price can become an exit opportunity. Underwater buyers who simply want their money back can turn into sellers on the way up, which may cap recoveries in the near term.

data.title: Inflation Slides in France, Spain on Declining Fuel Prices — 4th Update
data.description:
By Ed Frankl and Paul Hannon

The annual rate of inflation in France and Spain fell more sharply than expected in November as fuel prices declined, while the eurozone economy grew less rapidly than previously estimated in the three months through September.

Investors expect the European Central Bank to raise its key interest rate next month for a third time since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran. But the central bank has said it will be "data-dependent" in its policy decisions, and the latest readings from the eurozone economy point to weaker inflationary pressures.

Consumer prices in the eurozone's second-largest economy were 3.2% higher than in the same month of 2025, a lower annual rate of inflation than the 3.7% recorded in October, France's statistics office said Friday. Economists polled last week by The Wall Street Journal expected a 3.6% rate of inflation.

In Spain, figures published Friday showed the annual rate of inflation also dropped sharply in November, to 4.1% from 4.9% in October.

Oil prices have fallen since the outcome of U.S. midterm elections fueled hopes of a lasting resolution to the conflict, although they remain above prewar levels. As a result, prices of gasoline and other fuels have declined.

However, European natural gas prices remain near multiyear highs, which will keep household energy prices elevated throughout the colder winter months.

The ECB has raised its key rate twice so far this year, judging that the surge in energy prices was too great to ignore. Investors are primed for another hike before the end of the year.

The EU said last week that it expects French inflation to peak at 4.3% in the first quarter of 2027 due to further increases in energy prices and how they pass through into food and services.

Yet incoming data shows few signs of those energy costs spilling over into other parts of the economy. Services inflation in France fell in November due to a sharp decrease in prices for accommodation and transport services.

Revised figures for economic growth in the three months through September indicate that the eurozone economy has been less resilient in the face of higher energy prices than previously estimated.

The French statistics agency on Friday said the country's gross domestic product sank 0.2% in the third quarter, having previously estimated the drop at 0.1%. Consumer spending was also flat in October. Surveys of purchasing managers for November showed steady economic growth in Germany, while there was a deepening downturn in activity in France.

"A weakening labor market and growing fears of unemployment will keep households cautious. At the same time, weak demand and a lack of visibility will continue to weigh on business investment. The outlook for 2027 remains very gloomy," Charlotte de Montpellier, an economist at ING, wrote in a note to clients.

Earlier this week, Germany's statistics agency cut its estimate for third-quarter growth. Meanwhile, eurozone business sentiment slipped this month, according to separate data published Friday.

Amid those signs of weakening inflationary pressures, the ECB's own survey of 19,000 consumers between Oct. 1 and Nov. 2 yielded some concerning news for policymakers. It found that households expected prices to rise by 3.5% over the coming 12 months, up from 3.1% in September.

However, expectations may fall back in response to November's inflation figures, although the next survey won't be released until early next year and the ECB announces its policy decision on Dec. 17.

data.title: Why Enigma Investment CIO is avoiding large private banks despite recent rally
data.description:
Viraj Mehta, CIO of Enigma Investment Partners is steering clear of large private sector banks, citing declining year-on-year growth and intensifying competition from public sector lenders.

Despite private financials leading a sharp market recovery in November—surging 17 to 20% in a matter of months after a prolonged lull—Mehta views the move as a temporary bounce rather than the start of a sustained rerating.

"Any company which is structurally losing or reducing their growth year on year, we will not be very keen on buying," Mehta said. He pointed to slowing growth at HDFC Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank, and to a certain extent ICICI Bank, though he acknowledged the latter has been a "little bit of an outlier."

The historical advantage private lenders held over their state-owned peers has diminished. Mehta noted that the structural tailwinds private banks previously enjoyed, which were driven by the broken balance sheets of public sector undertakings (PSUs), no longer exist.

"PSU balance sheets are really, really pristine, so the competition is extremely high," he explained.

Watch the full conversation here

Consequently, Mehta characterised the recent surge in private banking stocks as a "one-off" run-up following five or more years of underperformance. Questioning whether the sector is entering a structural uptrend, he concluded: "We are not sure on that. So, we would definitely stay away."

data.title: ECB's gender gap set to widen further after Lagarde exit
data.description:
Key points:
  • ECB set to fall to bottom of global rankings for gender balance
  • Women to be outnumbered 26-1 on top policymaking body
  • Diverse committees less prone to groupthink, studies find
  • National governments keep sending men to Frankfurt

By Balazs Koranyi and Francesco Canepa

The European Central Bank is on course to become the most male-dominated major central bank in the world when President Christine Lagarde leaves in February, a jarring outcome for an institution that has spent years promoting gender balance.

The departure of Lagarde, a vocal advocate of greater female representation, and fellow board member Isabel Schnabel will leave just one woman among the ECB's 27 policymakers — a lower proportion than at Saudi Arabia's central bank.

The comparison is uncomfortable for an institution that has made gender diversity a hallmark of the Lagarde era. And research suggests the consequences can extend beyond appearance, with studies linking more diverse monetary policy committees to broader debate and even different responses to inflation.

"An institution whose decisions affect 350 million Europeans cannot afford to ignore half of the available talent," said Stéphanie Yon-Courtin, who sits on the European Parliament committee that oversees the ECB. "Without calling for strict parity at all costs, we are far from where we should be."

A Reuters analysis of 20 major central banks found that women hold about 28% of seats on their top policymaking bodies.

The Reserve Bank of Australia, chaired by Michele Bullock, has the highest female representation, with women holding six of nine seats. New Zealand and Britain also have female majorities.

The Saudi Central Bank has one woman on its eight-strong board, a higher proportion than even the two women currently among the ECB's 27 policymakers. From February, French nominee Laurence Boone, Schnabel's replacement, is expected to be the lone woman on the Governing Council.

MORE THAN A BAD LOOK

Research suggests the composition of policymaking committees can affect how they operate.

A study of three decades of US Federal Reserve deliberations found that more gender-balanced committees engaged in broader discussions, examined a wider range of issues and were more likely to challenge prevailing views.

Indeed, that is one reason central bankers increasingly expect diversity from the institutions they supervise.

Scholars from Bocconi University and Trinity College Dublin who studied monetary policy decisions across 90 countries between 2001 and 2017 meanwhile found that policy bodies with a higher share of women tended to adopt a more aggressive stance when inflation rose quickly.

"In a male-dominated field, women may feel pressure to demonstrate that their presence on a committee will not soften policy," Davide Romelli, a professor at Trinity and one of the authors of the study, said.

"It is also possible that women perceived as more hawkish stand out or are more likely to be appointed to central bank boards to bolster credibility."

Other studies in Europe and the United States have found that women tend to have higher inflation expectations than men, partly because of greater exposure to prices of food and other household necessities.

NATIONAL APPOINTMENTS DRIVE IMBALANCE

The ECB itself has little control over the gender balance of its top ranks.

Under Lagarde, the bank introduced targets and steadily increased the share of women among staff and management. Around 40% of senior managers are now women, the bank says, and roughly half of appointments and promotions go to women. The ECB declined to comment further.

The bigger obstacle is the way the Governing Council is assembled.

Twenty-one of its 27 members are national central bank governors chosen separately by euro zone countries whose governments' main focus is domestic.

In nearly three decades, only one woman has served on the Governing Council as a national central bank governor: Chrystalla Georghadji of Cyprus.

The six-member ECB Executive Board is selected by a different process and has maintained stronger female representation. Euro zone governments choose its members collectively after consulting the European Parliament.

France's nominee, Boone, is likely to become the sixth woman to serve on the Executive Board next year.

The European Parliament cannot veto appointments, but has repeatedly criticised the ECB's lack of diversity.

Yon-Courtin said she and other lawmakers would use upcoming confirmation hearings to express their frustration.

"It will also be an opportunity for me and other MEPs to urge, once again, heads of state and government to put forward gender-balanced shortlists every time," she said.

LEAKY PIPELINE IN ECONOMICS

The dominance of men at the ECB also reflects a broader shortage of women in top economics roles.

The Women in Economics Initiative estimates that women account for roughly a quarter of leaders at economics think tanks, university departments, major companies and international economic institutions, while only about one in seven central bank governors and finance ministers is a woman.

"We have a roughly equal number of men and women entering economic studies at university, but this pipeline is then eroded along the way," said Maria Demertzis, a professor at the European University Institute.

Today's pool of senior candidates also reflects an economics profession that was considerably more male-dominated when many began their careers.

There are signs that the pipeline is improving.

Germany, France, Italy and Spain have appointed female deputy central bank governors in recent years, while the number of women serving as alternates on the ECB's Governing Council has doubled during the Lagarde era.

Progress can be fragile, however. Research on central banks within the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development found that women were more likely to replace another woman than to succeed a man, suggesting gains in representation can quickly unravel when female policymakers like Lagarde and Schnabel leave.

data.title: Trump backs Iraqi leader's efforts to assert more state authority
data.description:
Key points:
  • Trump says he backs Zaidi's bid to extend state authority
  • Oil is at the heart of crackdown against Iran's alliies, Kurds
  • Iraq says oil smuggling deprives state coffers of revenues

US President Donald Trump on Friday backed the Iraqi leader's drive to assert state control, including stopping the smuggling of Iraqi oil, moves that put Baghdad in direct confrontation with Iran's militia allies and Kurdish authorities.

"We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state," Trump said in a Truth Social post.

The post appeared shortly after Iraqi government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said Baghdad considered crude oil exports that bypass state oil marketer SOMO to be smuggling as the proceeds do not reach the state treasury, the state news agency reported.

Speaking to the Iraqi state news agency, Aboudi added that Iraq lost an estimated $100 billion to oil smuggling through its Kurdistan region from 2008 to 2025.

It was unclear how the government calculated the figure.

Iraq is hoping to attract wide-scale foreign investment in its often struggling economy.

Iraq on Thursday closed two border crossings in the Kurdistan region, one with Syria and one with Iran, after Zaidi ordered federal authorities to take control of crossings run by the semi-autonomous regional government.

Thousands of Kurds protested on Thursday against Zaidi's moves to put oilfields under federal control and deploy federal troops along the region's international borders.

ARMED GROUPS HAVE AMASSED POWER

The moves against the Kurds, just a week after Zaidi ordered a showdown against a heavily-armed Shi'ite militia aligned with Iran, Kataib Hezbollah, put Zaidi in confrontation with two major factions in a country where armed groups have amassed power over decades of ethno-sectarian civil war. Both crackdowns have been linked to alleged oil-smuggling rings.

Iraq's highest court ruled on Wednesday that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all international borders including in the Kurdistan region.

The court decision appears to be a victory for Zaidi, a 41-year-old multimillionaire businessman and political novice who came to power in a compromise just six months ago. But political analysts say it may yet prove difficult to implement measures that challenge entrenched interests.

Ties between Baghdad and the Kurds have often been strained over control of oil, money, territory and trade. The central government responded with force when Kurdistan held an independence referendum in 2017, though relations have lately grown calmer.

The Kurdistan Regional Government on Wednesday rejected what it called the "military language and threats" used in a statement from the spokesman for the Iraqi military announcing the new steps.

It said it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption and called for an end to oil smuggling across Iraq, one of the world's leading oil producers and an ally of both the United States and Iran.

In Zaidi's other major standoff, the prime minister ordered the army last week to prepare to enter Jurf al-Sakhar south of Baghdad, where the government accuses Kataib Hezbollah of running a smuggling operation. The group was initially defiant but agreed to let soldiers enter the city.

data.title: Russia's Gazprom, Turkey's Botas extend gas supply deal for three years
data.description:
Key points:
  • Contracted gas volumes remain unchanged
  • Russia remains Turkey's largest gas supplier in Europe
  • Russian gas imports fell 24% to 12 bcm in January-September

By Olesya Astakhova and Can Sezer

Russia's Gazprom and Turkish state energy company Botas have extended their gas supply contracts by three years, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Friday.

Turkey has become one of the largest buyers of Russian pipeline gas since the war in Ukraine fractured Moscow's trade and political ties with the European Union.

Russia supplies gas to Turkey via the Blue Stream and TurkStream pipelines on the bed of the Black Sea. Some of the fuel goes further to Southern, Central and Eastern Europe through regional pipelines.

Novak said contracted volumes remained unchanged but provided no further details. He also said that Russia's largest liquefied natural gas producer, Novatek, has signed a contract to supply LNG to Turkey starting from January.

"The extension covers the same volumes as before," he said about the deal between Gazprom and Botas.

"Novatek has also signed a contract for LNG supplies starting January 1, 2027. Volumes are still small, but there is potential for growth," he added.

A major market for natural gas, despite a decrease in consumption in recent years, Turkey imports almost all its annual consumption of approximately 55 billion cubic metres.

Russia is Turkey's largest gas supplier, providing more than a third of its imports.

Imports from Russia were 21 bcm last year, according to Turkey's energy watchdog, and was 12 bcm for the January-September period, down 24% from the same time in 2025.

Turkey said in December it had agreed to extend for one year Russian gas import contracts covering 22 billion cubic metres annually.

Novak also said Russia had supplied more than 20 million metric tons of fuel, mainly diesel, to Turkey since the start of 2026.

data.title: AM Markets Need to Know: Trump disputes GDP, OPEC pressure, and more
data.description:
Stock index futures surged on Friday as Wall Street looked to close out a volatile week with a winning session, while Treasury yields moved higher following the Thanksgiving holiday break.

Here are the five news items investors should watch:

Trump challenges revised GDP figures: President Donald Trump called for an immediate investigation into the Commerce Department's revised third-quarter GDP figures, alleging that officials deliberately released inaccurate data ahead of the November midterm elections. The department revised annualized economic growth to 4.3% from its initial estimate of 3.4%. Trump described the revision as a "record setting error" but provided no evidence of deliberate manipulation.

U.S. pressured Venezuela and Iraq over OPEC: The Trump administration encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to consider leaving OPEC and blocked Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The pressure targeted two of the cartel's five founding members as Washington sought to encourage greater oil production. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman subsequently intervened to persuade the administration to drop its push against Venezuela.

Trump defends Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return: President Donald Trump said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was happy to return to his position, describing the executive's reinstatement as a "second term." Speaking at Mar-a-Lago, Trump defended his intervention despite bipartisan national security concerns. He offered no specific details when asked about the information supporting his confidence in Huang.

School districts push Google to disable AI features: Los Angeles Unified School District has disabled Google's AI-generated search summaries on school-issued devices, as districts demand permanent opt-out options for educational products. The move makes LAUSD, which serves approximately 500,000 students, the largest district to sideline the feature. The dispute could put pressure on Google's position in the U.S. education market.

Icahn Enterprises faces mounting refinancing pressure: Icahn Enterprises faces growing debt concerns after warning that it may not be able to refinance $1.4B of bonds due in May on acceptable terms, or at all. Yields on the bonds have climbed above 14% from ~ 6% three months ago, while some 2029 notes have reportedly topped 30%. Its major holding, CVR Energy , has also lost approximately 46% since agreeing to acquire two refineries.

data.title: Hackers reportedly breach US Air Force Cloud One system
data.description:
Key points:
  • Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.
  • The intrusion at Cloud One was ‌discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, sources told Reuters, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. 
  • In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it "does not comment on the ​security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems ​and mission capabilities."
  • Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force's ⁠IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft , Amazon , Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay ​or logistics and maintenance.
  • SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. Cloud One is among the US military's biggest cloud platforms, sources said. "A breach here is a big deal, the report added. Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military's cyber force, to assess the damage.
  • The discovery of the hack has reportedly led to a range of disruption. The report also said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused. Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. According to one source some users had their administrator rights revoked.

data.title: Stocks Poised to End Week Strong as Investors Take Break From AI Jitters — WSJ
data.description:
By Joe Stonor

The artificial-intelligence trade looks set to stage a rebound when the U.S. market opens for a shortened trading session Friday, capping another roller-coaster week for stocks.

Nasdaq-100 futures were trading 2.7% higher, while contracts tied to the S&P 500 and the Dow industrials rose 1.9% and 1.3%, respectively. Stocks tied to AI, from chip makers to data-center companies and Claude maker Anthropic, rallied in premarket trading.

It has been a choppy week in markets: After an epic rally on news of Jensen Huang's return as CEO of Nvidia, jitters around AI crept back in, knocking stocks lower. Investors now seem to be setting those concerns aside.

"There are so many signs of exhaustion of selling," said Gerry Fowler, an equity strategist at UBS. "You don't need anyone to choose to buy the market for it to go up. At these levels, you only need volatility to be slightly lower, and risk-control funds start to buy."

Trading is thin around the Thanksgiving break, Fowler said, meaning even a limited uptick in stock buying can translate into healthy-looking gains. U.S. markets were closed Thursday and will open for a shortened session Friday.

All three major indexes stand to extend gains of roughly 4% so far this week. But the AI trade isn't out of the woods yet, XTB research director Kathleen Brooks said.

"The fundamental problems surrounding the AI trade remain," Brooks said. "The questions that caused the market panic are still unanswered, for example, concerns about the profitability of the AI trade and financing costs."

The U.S. premarket gains followed a bullish session in Asia. South Korea's tech-dominated Kospi index jumped 4.3%, while stocks in Shanghai and Hong Kong rose after Chinese authorities reiterated their support for capital markets. European stocks also climbed, with AI-related stocks leading the charge.

Investors' renewed appetite for risk also sparked a rally in precious metals, which had tracked the recent AI selloff to hit their lowest levels of the year. Silver contracts jumped more than 10%, while gold futures gained close to 4% to trade around $3,680 a troy ounce.

U.S. Treasurys weakened amid hardened expectations for Federal Reserve rate increases in the coming months. Benchmark 10-year yields rose to trade above 4.9%. Yields rise when bond prices fall. The Fed enters a blackout period on Saturday ahead of its December meeting, where a quarter-point rise is broadly seen as a given, according to CME FedWatch.

A continued uptick in oil prices could strengthen the case for rate increases. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, drifted up to about $92.50 a barrel.
